name: Remediate kube-bench findings
objective: CKS › Cluster Setup + System Hardening (10% + 15%). Drill the kube-bench workflow harder than the exam: run it as a Job against node AND master, read [PASS]/[FAIL]/[WARN], then remediate every recurring finding — manifest & PKI file modes, the kubelet read-only port, the apiserver NodeRestriction plugin — plus a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Remediate a manifest-permission FAIL (scheduler)
questions.teach:
A recurring master `[FAIL]` (CIS 1.1.x) is a static pod manifest under `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` left group/world readable. CIS requires mode `0600` (`rw-------`); fix with `chmod 600 file`. Changing only the mode does NOT restart the pod, so it's safe live. On kind, reach the node with `docker exec $CP`.

**Gotcha:** `stat -c '%a'` drops the leading zero so `0600` prints `600` — leaving it `640` still leaks to the group and FAILs.
questions.prompt:
kube-bench flagged the kube-scheduler manifest on control-plane node `$CP`: setup loosened it to mode `644`. Set `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` on `$CP` to exactly mode `600`.

Target: `docker exec $CP stat -c '%a' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` prints `600`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $CP chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml   # 600 root:root
questions.eli5:
Think of each file's **permission mode** as who's allowed to peek inside a locked diary. The three digits in `600` are three groups of people: **owner / group / everyone-else**. `6` means "read + write," `4` means "read," `0` means "nothing."

- `600` = **only the owner** can read it. Nobody else. (`rw-------`)
- `644` = owner can read/write, but **the group AND the whole world can read it**. (`rw-r--r--`)

The kube-scheduler's **static pod manifest** holds sensitive startup flags, so the CIS inspector (kube-bench) says: this diary must be `600`. Someone loosened it to `644`, leaking it to everyone — that's a `[FAIL]` (CIS 1.1.x). The fix is one command: tighten the lock back down with `chmod 600`.

The lovely part: changing *who can read a file* does **not** restart the pod. The kubelet only reacts when the file's *contents* change. So this is a safe, live fix — no downtime.

On a **kind** cluster each node is really a Docker container, so you reach inside it with `docker exec $CP ...` to run the `chmod`.

**Watch out for:**

- **`stat` hides the leading zero.** Mode `0600` prints as `600`, and `0644` prints as `644` — don't panic at the "missing" zero.
- **`640` or `660` is still wrong.** Anything that lets the *group* read it (the middle digit above 0) still leaks and still FAILs. It must be exactly `600`.
- **chmod does NOT restart anything** — only editing the manifest's contents does. This fix is downtime-free.
- **It's on the control-plane node**, so use `docker exec $CP` (the `$CP` container), not a worker.
questions.deepDive:
## Remediating a manifest-permission FAIL (CIS 1.1.x) — full rundown

### Mental model
Static pod manifests under `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` are read by the kubelet to launch the control-plane pods. They embed sensitive flags (cert paths, bind addresses, admission config), so CIS section **1.1** requires them locked to mode `0600` (`rw-------`) and owned `root:root`. A loosened mode (e.g. `0644`) leaks the file to the group and the world — a kube-bench `[FAIL]`. The remediation is purely a **permission bit** change (`chmod`); it does not touch file content, so no pod restarts.

### Unix mode in 30 seconds
Three octal digits = **owner / group / other**. Each digit is the sum of read (4) + write (2) + execute (1).

| Mode | Symbolic | owner | group | other | CIS verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `600` | `rw-------` | rw | — | — | ✅ PASS |
| `640` | `rw-r-----` | rw | r | — | ❌ FAIL (group can read) |
| `644` | `rw-r--r--` | rw | r | r | ❌ FAIL (world-readable) |
| `660` | `rw-rw----` | rw | rw | — | ❌ FAIL (group can write) |

`stat -c '%a'` prints octal **without the leading zero**, so `0600` → `600`.

### The relevant CIS 1.1.x manifest controls
| CIS item | File | Required |
|---|---|---|
| 1.1.1 | `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` | `600` or stricter |
| 1.1.3 | `.../kube-controller-manager.yaml` | `600` or stricter |
| 1.1.5 | `.../kube-scheduler.yaml` | `600` or stricter |
| 1.1.7 | `.../etcd.yaml` | `600` or stricter |
| 1.1.2 / 1.1.4 / 1.1.6 / 1.1.8 | same files — **owner** | `root:root` |

(Item numbers shift slightly between benchmark versions; the *file → 600 root:root* rule is stable.)

### The fix (on kind)
```bash
# each kind node is a docker container; the control plane is $CP
docker exec $CP chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
docker exec $CP chown root:root /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml   # if owner drifted

# verify
docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
# -> 600 root:root
```

On a non-kind cluster you'd simply `ssh` to the control-plane node and run the same `chmod`/`chown`/`stat`.

### Why it's safe live
The kubelet watches these manifests and **re-creates the pod only when the file's content (mtime/hash) changes**. `chmod`/`chown` alter metadata, not content, so the running kube-scheduler pod is untouched. Contrast with editing the manifest body (next labs), which *does* trigger a restart.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`stat` drops the leading zero** — `600`, not `0600`. Don't add a digit trying to "fix" it.
- **Only `600` (or stricter like `400`) passes.** `640`/`644`/`660` all FAIL — any group/other read or group write leaks it.
- **Owner matters too.** A `600` file owned by a non-root user still FAILs the matching 1.1.x owner check; set `root:root`.
- **Don't restart the pod.** No `kubectl delete`, no manifest edit — a `chmod` is enough and restarting is needless risk.
- **Right node.** These files live on the **control plane** (`$CP`), not workers. `docker exec $W1` would find nothing.
- **Re-run kube-bench master** afterward to confirm the `[FAIL]` flipped to `[PASS]`.

### Quick reference
```bash
docker exec $CP chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml   # 600 root:root
```
Rule of thumb: **manifests & private keys → `600 root:root`; public certs → `644` is fine.**

questions.title: Protect PKI private-key permissions
questions.teach:
PKI private keys under `/etc/kubernetes/pki/` (CIS 1.1.19/1.1.21) are the crown jewels — anyone who reads `ca.key` can mint certs for any identity. kube-bench requires every `*.key` at mode `0600`. Fix with `chmod 600`; it changes only permission bits, so nothing restarts.

**Gotcha:** certs (`*.crt`) are public and may stay `0644`, but a `*.key` at `640` or `660` still leaks to the group and FAILs — keys must be exactly `600`.
questions.prompt:
kube-bench flagged `/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key` on `$CP`: setup loosened it to mode `644`. Set it back to exactly mode `600`.

Target: `docker exec $CP stat -c '%a' /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key` prints `600`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $CP chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key
docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key   # 600 root:root
questions.eli5:
PKI private keys are the **master keys to the whole kingdom**. The cluster's `ca.key` is the key that *signs* every ID card (certificate) in the cluster. If an attacker reads `ca.key`, they can forge an ID card for *anyone* — including the cluster admin. Game over.

So think of `ca.key` like the **master key to every lock in a building**, kept in the manager's private safe. The CIS inspector (kube-bench, CIS 1.1.19/1.1.21) insists: that safe must be openable by **only the owner** — mode `600`. Someone left it at `644`, meaning the whole building could peek at the master key. The fix is one `chmod 600` to slam the safe shut.

A handy distinction: there are two kinds of files side by side in `/etc/kubernetes/pki/`:

- **`*.crt` (certificates)** are like the *public* ID badges — anyone can see them, so `644` is fine.
- **`*.key` (private keys)** are the *secret* half — they must be `600`, locked to the owner.

Changing permissions touches only the lock, not the contents, so nothing restarts — it's a safe live fix. On kind, reach the control-plane container with `docker exec $CP`.

**Watch out for:**

- **`.key` must be exactly `600`.** `640` or `660` still lets the group read/write the secret key — that FAILs.
- **Don't "fix" the `.crt` files.** Public certs at `644` are correct; only the private `*.key` files need `600`.
- **`stat` shows `600`, not `0600`** — the leading zero is just hidden.
- **chmod doesn't restart anything** — content didn't change, so the control-plane pods keep running.
- **Control-plane node only** — `docker exec $CP`, not a worker.

## Protecting PKI private-key permissions (CIS 1.1.19 / 1.1.21) — full rundown

### Mental model
`/etc/kubernetes/pki/` holds the cluster's certificate authority and all component certs/keys. The **private keys** (`*.key`) are the crown jewels: `ca.key` signs every certificate in the cluster, so reading it lets an attacker mint a valid cert for any identity — including `system:masters`. CIS therefore demands every `*.key` be mode `0600` (owner-only). The matching **certificates** (`*.crt`) are public material and may stay world-readable (`0644`). The fix is a `chmod` — metadata only, so nothing restarts.

### The two CIS controls
| CIS item | Target | Required mode |
|---|---|---|
| 1.1.19 | `/etc/kubernetes/pki/` directory ownership | `root:root` |
| 1.1.20 | `/etc/kubernetes/pki/*.crt` (certs) | `644` or stricter |
| 1.1.21 | `/etc/kubernetes/pki/*.key` (private keys) | `600` or stricter |

> Numbers vary slightly by benchmark version, but the split is constant: **certs `≤644`, keys `≤600`, dir `root:root`.**

### cert vs key — why different modes
| File type | Example | Secret? | Allowed mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| Certificate | `ca.crt`, `apiserver.crt` | No (public) | `644` OK |
| Private key | `ca.key`, `apiserver.key` | **Yes** | `600` only |

A `*.key` at `640` leaks to the group; at `660` the group can also overwrite it. Both FAIL.

### The fix (on kind)
```bash
# single key
docker exec $CP chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key
docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key    # 600 root:root

# harden ALL private keys at once (idempotent, leaves certs alone)
docker exec $CP sh -c 'chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/pki/*.key'
docker exec $CP sh -c 'find /etc/kubernetes/pki -name "*.key" -exec stat -c "%a %n" {} \;'
```

### Why it's safe live
`chmod` changes permission bits, not file content. The kube-apiserver loaded these keys at startup and holds them in memory; it does not re-read `ca.key` on a metadata change, and the kubelet does not re-create any static pod. No restart, no downtime.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Keys must be exactly `≤600`.** `640`/`644`/`660` all FAIL. Don't confuse "it's readable, it works" with "it's compliant."
- **Don't tighten the `.crt` files below what tooling expects** — `644` on certs is correct and intended; forcing them to `600` is unnecessary and can break clients that read them unprivileged.
- **`stat -c '%a'` prints `600`, not `0600`.**
- **Owner check is separate.** A `600` key owned by non-root still FAILs the directory/owner control — keep `root:root`.
- **Right node.** PKI lives on the **control plane** (`$CP`). Workers have a kubelet client cert, not the CA key.
- **Globbing inside `docker exec`** needs a shell: `docker exec $CP sh -c 'chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/pki/*.key'` — the bare form won't expand the glob.

### Quick reference
```bash
docker exec $CP chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key
docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key   # 600 root:root
```
Rule: **`*.key` → 600, `*.crt` → 644, all owned `root:root`.**

questions.title: Harden the kubelet (read-only port)
questions.teach:
CIS 4.2.x: the kubelet can serve an **unauthenticated read-only port** (`10255`) that leaks pod/node metadata. kube-bench requires it disabled by setting `readOnlyPort: 0` in `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`. Editing the file isn't enough — run `systemctl restart kubelet` for it to take effect.

**Gotcha:** after the restart wait ~15-20s for the node to go `Ready` again; a bad edit can keep the kubelet down and leave the node `NotReady`. If it does, `docker exec $W1 journalctl -u kubelet -e --no-pager | tail` names the bad setting (🧰 Node toolbox).
questions.prompt:
On worker `$W1` the kubelet serves its read-only port (seeded as `readOnlyPort: 10255`). Edit `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` on `$W1` so `readOnlyPort: 0`, then restart the kubelet. Give the node ~20s to report `Ready`.

Target: the config on `$W1` has `readOnlyPort: 0` AND node `$W1` is `Ready`.
questions.hint: `docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`, then `docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
docker exec $W1 grep readOnlyPort /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml   # readOnlyPort: 0
docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl get node $W1   # wait ~20s for Ready

verification.description: node $W1 is still Ready after the kubelet restart

questions.eli5:
The kubelet is the agent running on each worker node. By default it can open a little side window called the **read-only port** (`10255`) where *anyone who can reach the node* — no password, no TLS — can peek at a live feed of what pods and node info are running. It's like a reception desk that hands out the building's guest list to any stranger who walks up. Handy once upon a time, a leak today.

The CIS inspector (kube-bench, CIS 4.2.x) says: **board up that window.** You do it by editing the kubelet's settings file, `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`, and setting `readOnlyPort: 0`. Zero means "off."

But here's the key twist, different from the file-permission fixes: **editing the config file does nothing by itself.** The kubelet already read its settings when it started up; it won't notice your change until you tell it to re-read them. So you must **restart the kubelet** (`systemctl restart kubelet`). On kind, both the edit and the restart happen inside the node container via `docker exec $W1`.

After the restart the node briefly drops offline and shows `NotReady` — that's normal. Give it ~20 seconds and it comes back `Ready`.

**Watch out for:**

- **The edit alone isn't enough — you MUST restart the kubelet** or the port stays open and it still FAILs.
- **A bad edit can keep the kubelet down**, leaving the node stuck `NotReady`. If it doesn't recover after ~20s, run `docker exec $W1 journalctl -u kubelet -e --no-pager | tail` — it names the bad setting (the Node toolbox).
- **It must be exactly `0`.** Any other number leaves the port open.
- **This is a worker-node fix** (`$W1`), not the control plane.
- Don't confuse *this* (turning the port off, a content change) with the *previous* idea of just changing file permissions — this one needs a restart.
questions.deepDive:
## Hardening the kubelet read-only port (CIS 4.2.x) — full rundown

### Mental model
The kubelet can expose an **unauthenticated, no-TLS read-only port** (default `10255`). Anyone who can reach the node on that port can scrape `/pods`, `/metrics`, and node/spec info without credentials — a reconnaissance goldmine. CIS requires it **disabled** by setting `readOnlyPort: 0` in the kubelet config. Unlike a file-permission fix, this is a **content** change to the kubelet's config, so it only takes effect after the kubelet process re-reads it — i.e. a `systemctl restart kubelet`.

### The control
| CIS item | Setting | Required | Default if unset |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4.2.x | `readOnlyPort` in `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` | `0` (disabled) | `0` on modern installs, but kube-bench wants it **explicitly** `0` |

Any non-zero value (e.g. `10255`) enables the insecure port and FAILs.

### The fix (on kind, worker `$W1`)
```bash
# 1. set readOnlyPort: 0 in the kubelet config
docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml

# 2. confirm the edit
docker exec $W1 grep readOnlyPort /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml   # readOnlyPort: 0

# 3. RESTART the kubelet so it re-reads config
docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet

# 4. wait ~15-20s, then confirm the node recovered
kubectl get node $W1     # Ready
```

### The config file
`/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` is a `KubeletConfiguration` object. Relevant top-level keys:
```yaml
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
readOnlyPort: 0            # <- CIS 4.2.x
authentication:
  anonymous:
    enabled: false        # related hardening (separate lab step)
authorization:
  mode: Webhook
```

### Why a restart is required (and file-perm fixes aren't)
| Change type | Example | Restart needed? | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Metadata** | `chmod 600 config.yaml` | No | kubelet doesn't re-read on metadata change |
| **Content** | `readOnlyPort: 0` | **Yes** | kubelet parses config only at startup |

### When the node stays NotReady
A malformed edit (bad YAML, wrong indentation, invalid value) makes the kubelet **fail to start**, so the node stays `NotReady`. Diagnose:
```bash
docker exec $W1 journalctl -u kubelet -e --no-pager | tail -n 40
# look for: "failed to load Kubelet config file", a YAML parse error, or an invalid field
docker exec $W1 systemctl status kubelet --no-pager
```
Fix the config, `systemctl restart kubelet`, wait again.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Edit without restart → still FAILs.** The running kubelet keeps the old value until restarted. This is the single most common miss.
- **Must be exactly `0`.** `10255` or any other number leaves it enabled.
- **Node goes `NotReady` for ~15-20s** on every kubelet restart — that's expected, not a failure. Only worry if it doesn't recover.
- **Don't confuse the two 4.x families:** `readOnlyPort: 0` (this, 4.2.x content) vs. `chmod 600` on `config.yaml` (4.1.9 file perms — a different step, no restart).
- **Worker node.** This is a kubelet/worker control (`$W1`), not the control plane.
- `sed` anchored with `^readOnlyPort:` only matches a top-level key — correct, since it's not nested.

### Quick reference
```bash
docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl get node $W1          # wait ~20s for Ready
# if NotReady:
docker exec $W1 journalctl -u kubelet -e --no-pager | tail
```

questions.title: Harden the apiserver (NodeRestriction)
questions.teach:
CIS 1.2.x: `NodeRestriction` is a kube-apiserver admission plugin that limits each kubelet to modifying **only its own Node and bound Pods**. Enable it in the `--enable-admission-plugins` flag — a comma-separated list, so append `,NodeRestriction` and keep the others.

**Gotcha:** the kubelet recreates the pod on save (no `kubectl apply`), but a typo takes the apiserver down for ~15-30s — edit carefully and wait.
questions.prompt:
Setup removed `NodeRestriction` from the apiserver's `--enable-admission-plugins`. Edit `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` on `$CP` so the flag includes `NodeRestriction` again (keep any other plugins), then wait for the apiserver to come back.

Target: the running kube-apiserver has `NodeRestriction` in `--enable-admission-plugins`.
questions.hint: `docker exec $CP ...` edit the manifest: add the line `- --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction` under the kube-apiserver command args (or append `,NodeRestriction` to an existing value). Wait ~20s for the apiserver to restart.
questions.solution:
# Setup removed the flag line, so add it back under the kube-apiserver args:
docker exec $CP sed -i '/^    - kube-apiserver$/a\    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# (If the flag already exists with other plugins, instead append ,NodeRestriction to its value.)
# Wait ~20s for the apiserver to restart, then verify:
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins
questions.eli5:
Every worker node runs a kubelet, and each kubelet has credentials to talk to the cluster's brain (the apiserver). Without a guard rail, a compromised kubelet could reach out and tamper with *other* nodes or *other* pods — far beyond its own patch of the cluster. That's a big blast radius if one node gets hacked.

**NodeRestriction** is that guard rail. It's a bouncer standing at the apiserver door (an **admission plugin**) whose one job is: "If a request comes from a kubelet, it may only touch *its own* Node object and the Pods scheduled onto it — nothing else." So a hijacked worker can't vandalize the whole cluster.

You switch the bouncer on in the apiserver's settings file (`kube-apiserver.yaml`) by making sure `NodeRestriction` is listed in the `--enable-admission-plugins` flag. Important detail: that flag is **one comma-separated list** of plugins. So you don't replace it — you **add** `NodeRestriction` to whatever's already there (or add the whole flag back if setup deleted it).

The nice part: the apiserver is a **static pod**, so the moment you save the file, the kubelet automatically restarts it with the new setting — no `kubectl apply` needed.

**Watch out for:**

- **It's a comma-separated list.** Keep the existing plugins and append `,NodeRestriction` — don't clobber the others by overwriting the flag.
- **Saving auto-restarts the apiserver.** A typo takes the apiserver DOWN for ~15-30s (and `kubectl` stops responding during that gap) — edit carefully and wait for it to return.
- **Don't run `kubectl apply`** — the kubelet picks up the manifest change on its own; applying it as a resource is wrong for a static pod.
- **Control-plane node only** (`$CP`), via `docker exec`.
- Verify on the *running* pod, not just the file: `kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins`.
questions.deepDive:
## Enabling the NodeRestriction admission plugin (CIS 1.2.x) — full rundown

### Mental model
Admission plugins are gatekeepers that run **inside the apiserver** after authn/authz but before an object is persisted. **NodeRestriction** limits what a kubelet (identity `system:node:<nodeName>`, group `system:nodes`) may do: it may modify **only its own Node object** and **only the Pods bound to it**. Without it, a compromised node's kubelet credentials could edit other nodes, label-spoof, or escalate. CIS 1.2.x requires it enabled via the apiserver's `--enable-admission-plugins` flag. The apiserver is a **static pod**, so editing its manifest auto-restarts it.

### The control
| CIS item | Flag | Required value |
|---|---|---|
| 1.2.x | `--enable-admission-plugins` | must **include** `NodeRestriction` |

It works together with the kubelet's **Node authorizer** (`--authorization-mode=Node`); NodeRestriction is the admission half that enforces the write scope.

### Key fact: it's ONE comma-separated flag
```
--enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity,...
```
You must **preserve existing plugins** and append, not overwrite. Two scenarios:

**A) flag already present with other plugins** — append:
```yaml
- --enable-admission-plugins=PodSecurity,NodeRestriction
```

**B) flag missing entirely (as in this lab)** — add the line under the command args:
```bash
docker exec $CP sed -i '/^    - kube-apiserver$/a\    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction' \
  /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
```

### The manifest shape
```yaml
# /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction   # <- here
    - --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
    # ...other flags...
```

### Static-pod restart behaviour
| Action | Effect |
|---|---|
| Save the manifest | kubelet detects the content change and **re-creates** the apiserver pod |
| `kubectl apply` | **Wrong** — static pods aren't managed via the API; the mirror pod is read-only |
| Typo / bad flag | apiserver crash-loops; `kubectl` is unreachable for the gap |

### Verify (on the running pod)
```bash
# wait ~20-60s after saving, then:
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins
# or from the node, confirm the flag is actually in the process:
docker exec $CP grep enable-admission-plugins /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
```

### When the apiserver won't come back
```bash
# the mirror pod may be gone; inspect the container/logs on the node
docker exec $CP crictl ps -a | grep apiserver
docker exec $CP sh -c 'crictl logs $(crictl ps -a -q --name kube-apiserver | head -1)' 2>&1 | tail
# common cause: typo in the flag name or a stray character broke YAML
```
Fix the manifest; the kubelet retries automatically.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Don't overwrite other plugins.** `--enable-admission-plugins` is a single list — appending `,NodeRestriction` must keep the rest.
- **No `kubectl apply`.** It's a static pod; just save the file on the node.
- **Saving = restart.** Expect a 15-60s apiserver outage; `kubectl` errors during it are normal.
- **Verify on the running pod,** not only the file — a manifest edit that never restarted (or crash-looped) isn't actually in effect.
- **Needs `Node` authorizer too** for full effect (`--authorization-mode=Node,RBAC`); on kubeadm clusters that's already set.
- **Control-plane node** (`$CP`) only.
- **Indentation matters** in the `sed` insert — manifest args are indented; a misaligned line breaks YAML.

### Quick reference
```bash
# add the flag back (setup removed it)
docker exec $CP sed -i '/^    - kube-apiserver$/a\    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction' \
  /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# wait, then verify on the running pod
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins
```
